title: The discovery of the microwave
subtitle: By accident
subject: sciences
description: In 1945, an engineer noticed that his candy bar had melted near a radar. From this observation the microwave oven was born.

hero.hook: A melted chocolate bar… and modern cuisine changes.

blocks.text: In **1945**, in the United States, engineer **Percy Spencer** works on radars. One day he notices that the candy bar in his pocket has melted. Not because of body heat: because of radar waves.
He tests with corn: the popcorn pops. The idea of ​​an oven that heats differently was born.

blocks.caption: World War II radars already used microwaves.

blocks.text: **microwaves** are electromagnetic waves, like radio light, but more "energetic" than many conventional radio waves. During the war, they were mainly used for radar to detect planes and boats.
Spencer understands that they can also agitate water and fats in food... and therefore heat it.

blocks.caption: The first commercial microwave oven was the size of a cabinet.

blocks.text: The first commercial model, the **Radarange**, was released around **1947**. It is huge, expensive, and mainly intended for restaurants or boats. It will take decades to miniaturize it and make it affordable for homes.
At first, some were afraid that the oven would “make the food radioactive.” False: microwaves heat up, they do not make you radioactive.

sections.title: How does it really heat up?

blocks.text: Microwaves mainly vibrate water molecules (and a little fats and sugars). This agitation creates **heat inside** the food, not just on the surface like a pan.
This is why a dish can be hot on the outside and lukewarm in the center if it is thick: the waves do not penetrate infinitely deep.
From the 1970s-1980s, the microwave oven entered millions of kitchens. It changes habits: reheat quickly, ready meals, faster life.
The microwave was born from a coincidence observed by Percy Spencer near a radar. The waves mainly agitate the water in the food and heat it from the inside.
